title: Sol Plaatje's Mafeking Weekly and the Advertisers Who Did Not Pay
dek: From 1901 Sol Plaatje built Koranta ea Becoana into a national Setswana-English paper with its own press, then struggled for years to keep it alive.

story.event: Building and losing a Setswana-English weekly in Mafeking
story.summary: After the siege of Mafeking, with promotion in the civil service closed to him by the colour bar, Sol Plaatje became editor of Koranta ea Becoana, a small Setswana supplement bought by Silas Molema, and by 1903 had made it an eight-page Setswana-English weekly with its own printing plant. Limited literacy and advertisers slow to pay kept it short of money, and it closed after about seven years, in 1908 or 1909 by different accounts. In 1910 Plaatje started again in Kimberley with Tsala ea Becoana, which faced the same financial strain.
paragraphs: When the siege of Mafeking ended in 1900, Sol Plaatje was twenty-three. He had spent it as interpreter to the court and confidential clerk to the official running Native affairs, writing weekly reports the military valued. A Pretoria editor who knew him then wrote in 1910 that, but for the colour bar, Plaatje would probably have held an important post in the Native Affairs department. With that door shut, he turned to journalism.

The paper he took on was small. Koranta ea Becoana, the Bechuana Gazette, had been started by G. H. Whales, editor of the Mafeking Mail, as a one-page Setswana supplement with a circulation of about 500. Silas Molema, of a leading Barolong family, bought it so that Plaatje could edit it. Under Plaatje it became a weekly in Setswana and English; he doubled its pages, appointed newsagents and went after advertisers. By the end of 1902 it ran to eight pages and sold about 2,000 copies across the country, and by 1903 Molema and Plaatje had their own printing plant and office in Mafeking.

Koranta was moderate in tone but not quiet. It criticised British rule in the Transvaal and Orange River colonies, where Africans faced violent police and courts that did not protect them, and argued that the rights Africans held in the Cape, including the vote, should be extended to the rest of the country. In a letter Plaatje wrote over Molema's signature, he called the paper "the only channel through which the truth can be disseminated to the native population of Bechuanaland."

That did not pay the bills. Circulation was limited where few could read, and Plaatje's surviving letters from these years record a long struggle to keep the paper going while advertisers, De Beers among them, were slow to pay. Koranta lasted about seven years; accounts put its end in 1908 or mid-1909.

Plaatje did not stop. By June 1910 he had moved his family to Kimberley and launched Tsala ea Becoana. The money troubles came with him; it closed in 1912 and was followed by Tsala ea Batho. That year he became the first secretary-general of the South African Native National Congress.

quote.text: My roof’s a ruin, true; but light pours through the rent. I’m dust. But from my soil flowers blow, and yield sweet scent.
quote.locator: Book I, Section XVI, "‘Ali’s Forbearance" (ʿAli's reply to the warrior)
quote.source_title: The Mesnevi, tr. Sir James W. Redhouse, Project Gutenberg eBook #61724
quote.connection: In Rumi's telling, ʿAli admits the ruin and still finds light through the gap and flowers in the dust. Koranta's end did not erase what it had grown, but Plaatje's next paper met the same unpaid bills, and the verse does not say how often a person should rebuild on the same ground.

reflection: Plaatje's paper did not struggle because its writing was poor. Its troubles had more to do with how few people could read it, and how slowly some of those who owed it money paid. A worthwhile piece of work and a viable business are different things, and saying so is no insult to the work.

You may have days when what you are building feels both necessary and unaffordable. Plaatje kept going by starting again in a better-placed town with new backers, and by writing for other newspapers to cover his costs. Both were part of keeping faith with the first idea, not a betrayal of it.
invitation: Name one piece of your work that is good but not yet paying its way. Write down one person who might help carry its cost, and leave the asking for another day.

sources.title: Solomon Tshekisho Plaatje
sources.supports: Born 9 October 1876; advancement in the civil service closed to him, he turned to journalism after the war; with financial backing from Silas Molema he established the first Setswana-English weekly, Koranta ea Becoana, in 1901; it existed under his editorship for six or seven years, after which he moved to Kimberley and started Tsala ea Becoana; his contributions to other papers; first Secretary-General of the SANNC

sources.title: Sol T Plaatje: Pariah In the Land of His Birth
sources.supports: Koranta ea Becoana dated 1901–1908; started by G. H. Whales of the Mafikeng Mail as a one-page Tswana supplement with an initial circulation of 500; bought by Silas Molema for Plaatje to edit; Plaatje increasing it to two pages, appointing newsagents and soliciting advertisements; eight pages and a national circulation of 2,000 by the end of 1902; printing plant and office set up by Molema and Plaatje the following year; modest size, moderate tone and low circulation in a population with limited literacy; criticism of British administration in the Transvaal and Orange River Colonies and the case for extending Cape rights and franchise

sources.title: Volume III-2: Sol Plaatje, reviews / resensies (reviews of Sol T. Plaatje: A Life in Letters, ed. Brian Willan and Sabata-mpho Mokae, 2020)

sources.title: Today in Kimberley's History: 2 July 1910, Sol Plaatje publishes Tsala ea Becoana for the first time

sources.title: Today in Kimberley's History: 19 April 1913, Sol Plaatje's newspaper becomes Tsala ea Batho
sources.supports: Continuing financial struggle; the last issue of Tsala ea Becoana on 8 June 1912; its renaming as Tsala ea Batho in April 1913; Plaatje earning small sums from contributions to the Pretoria News and the Diamond Fields Advertiser

research_notes: Dates are the main conflict. Start: South African History Online and Wikipedia give 1901; a Lucien van der Walt encyclopedia entry (read, not cited) says 1902; the SOAS blog dates Plaatje's editorship from 1902; the story says the siege ended in 1900 and gives 1902 for the paper's expansion, and the summary keeps 1901 for the founding. End: The Journalist gives 1901–1908; Wikipedia says the paper collapsed at the end of May 1909 because of financial difficulties; the 1910 Pretoria News profile reprinted in Native Life says it 'existed for seven years', SAHO 'six or seven years'; the SOAS blog (editing 1902–1905) and a HiPSA reviewer (1901–1904) give shorter spans that probably reflect surviving holdings or Plaatje's formal editorship. The story says 'about seven years' and 'in 1908 or mid-1909'. Cause of closure: the HiPSA review of Plaatje's collected letters (Willan and Mokae, 2020) describes his struggle to keep Koranta going as advertisers, including De Beers, were slow to pay; The Journalist notes low circulation where literacy was limited. A Kimberley local-history column also blames Plaatje's grasp of business economics; that judgement is not the founder's own or a court's, so it is left out. The 1910 Pretoria News profile called the paper 'very successful', a public view at odds with Plaatje's letters; the story relies on the letters. Tsala ea Becoana's first issue: the Kimberley column's headline says 2 July 1910 but its text says 18 June 1910; the story says 'by June 1910 ... launched'. The quotation from Plaatje's letter is taken from the HiPSA reviewer, who cites page 18 of A Life in Letters; the letter was signed in Molema's name. Ownership: Molema financed and owned the paper and Plaatje edited it, so funding is 'mixed' (a patron's capital plus sales and advertising). Primary documents (the Molema-Plaatje Papers at Wits and the SOAS digital collection, including a 1902 indent for printing machinery) were found but their pages do not load as text for the verifier. Rumi's lines are ʿAli's words about humility and forbearance; they are applied to the paper's closure by analogy.
